newsitem.title: USA: Muni groups pray for Senate relief on 'de minimis'.
newsitem.headline: Muni groups pray for Senate relief on 'de minimis'.

text.p: With U.S. House committee action on a tax bill complete, muni groups are marshaling forces to keep a rollback of the two percent de minimis rule for munis out of a Senate panel bill, lobbyists said Friday.

"The principal challenge right now is to keep the pro rata disallowance out of the Senate Committee mark(up bill)," Micah Green, executive vice president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, told Reuters.

The House Ways and Means Committee early this morning approved a broad tax plan that would scale back the two percent de minimis exemption for corporate holdings of muni bonds to a flat $1 million -- which lobbyists say renders the exemption largely meaningless.
Lobbyists say they now will focus on the Senate Finance Committee, which is expected to begin voting on a tax package June 19.
Chairman William Roth, R-Del., is expected to circulate a draft measure shortly. Muni groups are already working furiously to keep a de minimis repeal clause out.

"We're trying to crank up the grass roots, get the issuers involved," Green said. "It's working very well, but we won't know until we see the mark," he said, referring to Roth's bill. "Once it's in the mark, it's very difficult to get things out," Green said.

PSA vice president Michael Decker said another major disappointment is Archer's agreement this week to drop a proposal to repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax, which would have beefed up demand for long-term munis by property and casualty companies.

Decker said the Ways and Means bill does have some positives, particularly an increase in the $150 million volume cap on the amount of tax-exempt bonds that private, non-profit colleges may have outstanding, from $150 million to $200 million over five years.

Bond lobbyists are betting that a 501(c)(3) provision will land in Roth's bill since Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, N.Y., top Democrat on Roth's panel, already introduced a measure to wipe out the $150 million cap altogether.
The Ways and Means bill also would liberalize rules for issuance of mortgage revenue bonds in areas declared as disasters for first-time homebuyers.

And it includes some minor bond simplification measures offered this spring by President Clinton, but the big-ticket arbitrage relief provisions sought by bond groups did not make it in Archer's bill.
The Government Finance Officers Association this week issued an "Urgent Legislative Alert" asking localities to lobby for Senate panel consideration of two proposals.
One would increase the small issuer arbitrage rebate exception from $5 million to $10 million.
Another would provide a safe harbor from arbitrage rules for issuers that reasonably expect to spend 15 percent of proceeds within 12 months and 95 percent within three years of issuance.

Senate finance panel member Bob Graham, D-Fla., emerged as a key ally for issuers on June 11 with an 11-page memo urging finance panel members to include those two and other muni bond simplification provisions in any Senate tax package.
